_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 1 Precise Instructions. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (exactly what you say; what, how big, where; a linear algorithm; only the steps you need; building and drawing). Every picture of what Robo actually draws is the LESSON'S OWN drawing, given the list of instruction ids it was told - ART.drawing(house, [walls, roof-corner]) puts the roof in the corner, ART.scene(tea, [water]) paints the puddle and captions it, ART.scene(tower, [red, blue]) stacks the bricks - so the film draws no picture of a mistake of its own.
title: Precise Instructions
subtitle: Grade 2 Computing
objectives: Know that an algorithm is a precise set of instructions.
Know how to develop precise sets of instructions to complete simple tasks, such as drawing a picture of a particular object or building a brick tower.
Identify the steps needed to undertake tasks, in order to develop simple algorithms.

beats.say: Tell Robo to draw a shape, and Robo draws any shape at all.
Say a big square in the middle, and you get exactly that.

at.square: a big square in the middle

beats.say: Robo can draw. But Robo does exactly what it is told, and nothing more.
You say: draw a shape. Robo draws a squiggle, and that is a shape.
A shape is any shape, anywhere. Robo did exactly what you said.
Try again. Say: draw a big square in the middle.

at.square: a big square in the middle

beats.say: That one is precise. It says what, how big, and where.
So an algorithm is a precise set of instructions, with nothing left to guess.
A precise instruction says what to draw, how big, and where.
Draw a big square in the middle. Robo draws the walls.

at.square: Draw a big square in the middle

beats.say: Say draw a roof somewhere, and Robo puts the roof anywhere it likes.
Say a triangle on top of the square, and the roof goes where a roof belongs.

at.triangle: a triangle on top of the square

beats.say: A small door at the bottom. A window on the wall, at the top left.

at.door: A small door at the bottom

beats.say: The sun in the top right of the sky. Nothing is left for Robo to guess.

at.sun: The sun in the top right

beats.say: A cup of tea has five steps. Making it is an algorithm too.
Step one: get a cup. Step two: put a tea bag in the cup.

at.bag: put a tea bag in the cup

beats.say: Step three: pour in the hot water. The tea goes brown.
Step four: add a little milk. Step five: stir it with a spoon.
Pour the water first and you get a puddle on the table.
Follow it exactly as it is written, one step after another. That is a linear algorithm.
Before you write an algorithm, work out which steps the task needs.
Taking a photo needs the tablet switched on, and the camera open.
Point it at the cat. Tap the round button. Look at your photo.
It does not need a coat, a song, or a watered plant.
A step the task does not need is a step that does not belong.

at.step: A step the task does not need

beats.say: Put the needed steps in order, and you have written an algorithm.
The same rule builds a tower. Robo puts the red brick down first.
Add a brick is vague: any brick, anywhere. Robo could give you any of these.
Put the blue brick on top of the red brick. Now only one tower fits.

at.blue: the blue brick on top of the red brick

beats.say: Precise steps, in the right order, and nothing that does not belong.
Precise means exact, with nothing left to guess. Vague leaves things to guess.
An algorithm is a precise set of instructions to do a job.
A linear algorithm is a straight line of steps. Follow every one.
Work out which steps the task needs, and leave the others out.
